supportingEvidence.title: White House Executive Order 14420: Declaring a National Emergency to Secure the United States Bulk-Power System
supportingEvidence.note: Primary source declares the emergency, explicitly cites rapid growth of data centers and artificial intelligence as magnifying dependence on reliable electricity, and authorizes restrictions and mitigation for risky foreign-produced bulk-power equipment, software, services and remote-access capabilities.

supportingEvidence.title: Reuters: Trump signs order banning some foreign equipment from U.S. energy grid
supportingEvidence.note: Independent reporting corroborates the executive action and describes the focus on foreign-manufactured grid equipment and cybersecurity/operational risk.

contradictingEvidence.title: Executive order requires case-specific risk determinations and reliability considerations
contradictingEvidence.note: The order is not a blanket ban on all foreign grid equipment. DOE must make risk determinations, may use mitigation, and must consider reliability, replacement availability and continuity before isolation or removal.

falsifier: Downgrade the thesis that this materially changes AI/grid infrastructure economics if DOE implementation remains narrow, few transactions or installed assets are restricted, replacement requirements do not affect procurement or lead times, and secure domestic grid supply does not become a binding constraint for data-center or AI infrastructure expansion.
title: U.S. declares bulk-power security emergency as AI and data-center electricity dependence rises
summary: Executive Order 14420 declares a national emergency over foreign supply and cyber risks in the U.S. bulk-power system. The White House explicitly ties the higher consequence of grid disruption to rapid growth in data centers, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and defense production, while authorizing DOE to restrict or mitigate risky foreign-produced equipment and associated digital capabilities.
delta: Add grid-security and equipment-origin risk as a first-class dependency of the AI infrastructure graph. Supersede the simpler model in which AI compute capacity depends mainly on GPUs, data centers and aggregate power availability: secure grid hardware, software, remote-access provenance and replacement lead times can now change project risk and procurement economics.
firstOrderImpacts: higher compliance and procurement scrutiny for foreign-produced transformers, inverters, control systems, software, firmware and remote-access services used in the bulk-power system
potential replacement, isolation or mitigation costs for risky installed equipment
greater strategic value for trusted domestic or allied grid-equipment supply chains as AI/data-center electricity demand rises
secondOrderImpacts: AI data-center expansion may become constrained not only by megawatts but by the security provenance and replacement lead time of grid equipment
grid-equipment manufacturers, cybersecurity vendors and supply-chain intelligence become more economically connected to the AI infrastructure buildout
Orbital/Operations intelligence can join data-center locations, transmission constraints, equipment origin and policy restrictions to identify infrastructure bottlenecks earlier
